answer.summary: Pfeffer says breaking rules can make you memorable and help disrupt industries because established rules tend to favor incumbents. He points to businesses doing things differently and to Jason Calacanis’s unconventional VC approach as examples.

sections.heading: Why breaking rules can build power
sections.content: Pfeffer gives two reasons: doing something unexpected makes you stand out and become memorable; and rules are mostly made by people favored by the existing system. In business, challenging those rules can mean disrupting an industry by doing something different from its incumbents.

sections.heading: Business examples
sections.content: Pfeffer illustrates disruption with Southwest Airlines avoiding the hub-and-spoke model, Amazon emphasizing exceptional customer service, and Whole Foods prioritizing fit with local tastes over optimizing store costs. He also describes Jason Calacanis as defying conventional VC wisdom: making many small bets rather than a few large ones, running a lean operation, and having no partners. Pfeffer connects Calacanis’s journalism background—asking smart people questions—to developing insight into the internet industry.

judgment.explanation: The answer accurately attributes both reasons to Pfeffer: breaking rules makes someone stand out and memorable, and established rules tend to favor those already advantaged. Its business examples are also supported by the cited context.
